title: Worn clothes
hookLine: as a person casts off worn clothes, the self casts off worn bodies

lines: CLOTHES AND THE ONE WHO WEARS THEM.
cards: A shirt with a frayed collar and thin elbows, worn so long it's soft as paper. Sooner or later it gets folded and let go.
The Bhagavad Gita, a Hindu scripture spoken on a battlefield, reaches for exactly that picture when it talks about death.
Krishna tells the warrior Arjuna that the self sets aside worn-out bodies the way a person sets aside worn-out clothes. And he says it to a man standing between two armies.

teach.b: First, the setting. Arjuna looks across the field and sees teachers and relatives in the other army. He puts down his bow, grieving before a single arrow has flown.
Krishna, his charioteer, whom many Hindus worship as God, begins to answer him. Second, the self.
Krishna says the self is never born and never dies; it is not slain when the body is slain. A little later he adds that weapons do not cut it and fire does not burn it. Third, the clothes.
Between those two teachings comes the picture.

teach.h: A GARB OF FLESH, SET ASIDE.
teach.b: In Edwin Arnold's old English verse: "So putteth by the spirit / Lightly its garb of flesh." Clothes wear thin; the one who wears them goes on. It's a household image for one of the hardest questions people ask.

teach.h: SAID TO A MAN ABOUT TO ACT.
teach.b: Some Hindu teachers read the verse as comfort, and as a teaching about what in a person lasts. But notice who hears it first: not a mourner at a funeral, a man about to act.

Krishna's point, in the poem, is that grief for bodies should not keep Arjuna from his duty. Some readers take the battlefield as a real war; others read it as a picture of the struggle inside a person.
Both hear the same verse about clothes.
And the week, looking back: death recalled with each breath, the charnel ground, strive on, no one to blame, rebirth, a last poem, and now worn clothes.

how: Hindus read and recite the Bhagavad Gita at home, in temples and in study groups, and verses from its second chapter, including this one, are sometimes recited in times of death and grief.

o: the Gita's picture of the self setting aside a worn body
the plain white garments mourners wear to a funeral
a Hindu custom of giving away a dead person's clothes

games.q: the battlefield and the verse — tap the pairs.
p: his charioteer, revered by many as God
cannot cut or burn the self

s: the worn-clothes picture comes from a funeral sermon
Krishna says it on a battlefield, to a warrior about to fight.
in the Gita, Krishna says weapons cannot cut the self
and fire does not burn it. it comes just after the clothes verse.
the verse says the body is worthless
it says worn bodies are set aside like worn clothes. the point is that the wearer goes on.

games.q: you're Arjuna. relatives and teachers stand in the other army, and your bow is on the ground. what does Krishna tell you about death?
o: that the people across the field aren't really there.
that the self isn't slain when the body is; it sets bodies aside like worn clothes.
that you should never grieve for anyone.
games.why: he teaches that the self is never born and never dies, and gives the picture of worn clothes. and he says it to move Arjuna to act.

practice: If there's an old piece of clothing nearby, take it in your hands; if not, rest a hand on your sleeve.
Fold it slowly, noticing the worn places, a thin spot, a loose thread, a softness that only comes from use, and breathe while you fold.
You don't have to think about death at all; just handle something worn, gently, and set it down.

wordCard.voice: Worn clothes: the Bhagavad Gita's picture of the self setting aside a worn body the way a person sets aside worn clothing. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit, the opening words of Bhagavad Gita 2.22: worn-out garments.

carryVoice: Your line: garb of flesh. Set aside lightly, in Arnold's old verse. See you tomorrow.
